curation.lead:
Brian Allen Benczkowski is a Washington attorney whose two-decade career alternated between Kirkland & Ellis and the U.S. Department of Justice. He served as Partner at K&E (2010–2017, 2020–2025), as Assistant Attorney General for the Criminal Division (2018–2020), and before that held senior staff roles under Deputy AG Mark Filip and AG Michael Mukasey during the George W. Bush administration. As AAG, he headed the division whose Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section (CEOS) holds federal jurisdiction over sex trafficking under 18 USC 1591 — the statute used to indict Jeffrey Epstein in July 2019 — yet his name does not appear in the 331,000+ DOJ document corpus related to the case.

Benczkowski's relevance to this investigation stems from his positioning at several institutional junctures. In 2007, as a DOJ legislative affairs official, he authored a letter arguing that prostitution-related offenses are historically state-level crimes — language that K&E later cited in its brief urging dismissal of the Epstein federal case. In 2008, he served as Chief of Staff to Deputy AG Filip when K&E partner Ken Starr wrote to Filip lobbying against the same prosecution. He later joined K&E, then returned to DOJ to head the Criminal Division under AG William Barr (another K&E alumnus), alongside Deputy AG Jeffrey Rosen (a 29-year K&E partner) — meaning all three of the most senior DOJ officials overseeing criminal enforcement came from the same firm that had defended Epstein.

His tenure also involved multiple ethics waivers to participate in prosecutions of K&E clients, a contested confirmation (51–48) after his representation of Alfa Bank was discovered in his FBI background file rather than his Senate questionnaire, and $847,500 in severance from K&E upon joining DOJ. He has since joined Boeing as VP and Assistant General Counsel for Government Operations.
curation.system_role: Benczkowski is a K&E partner and former DOJ Criminal Division chief whose career repeatedly placed him at the intersection of K&E and DOJ during periods relevant to the Epstein case. His documentary absence from the case files, despite heading the division with jurisdiction, remains unexplained.

sections.title: The Kirkland & Ellis Revolving Door
sections.content:
Benczkowski's career is structured around a single institutional axis: the passage between Kirkland & Ellis and the Department of Justice. His trajectory began in the George W. Bush DOJ, where he served as Staff Director and Senior Counsel in the Office of Legal Policy (2002–2004), Chief of Staff at ATF (2006–2007), Principal Deputy AAG for Legislative Affairs (2007–2008), and then Chief of Staff to both Deputy AG Mark Filip and AG Mukasey (2008–2009). After serving as Republican Staff Director on the Senate Judiciary Committee, he joined K&E as partner in 2010.

The Filip relationship warrants close attention. Filip, a K&E partner who became Deputy AG, was the highest DOJ official to review the Epstein Non-Prosecution Agreement. Benczkowski served as Filip's chief of staff during the period that K&E partner Ken Starr wrote to Filip lobbying to drop the Epstein federal case. After government service, Benczkowski and Filip were K&E co-counsel on major corporate defense matters including BP, Volkswagen, and Abbott Laboratories. When Benczkowski returned to DOJ as AAG in 2018, Filip remained at K&E defending Goldman Sachs and Boeing — cases where Benczkowski received ethics waivers to participate despite his former firm representing the defendants.

During his Criminal Division tenure (July 2018–July 2020), Benczkowski served alongside AG William Barr (K&E Of Counsel, 2009–2018, receiving $1.2M+ in compensation) and Deputy AG Jeffrey Rosen (K&E partner for 29 years, $4.57M in final-year compensation). All three of the most senior DOJ officials overseeing federal criminal enforcement were alumni of the same firm that had secured Epstein's 2008 non-prosecution agreement. Benczkowski received $847,500 in severance from K&E upon joining DOJ.

sections.title: Structural Entanglement with the Epstein Case
sections.content:
Benczkowski's connection to the Epstein case is indirect but touches several institutional nodes. The first documented link is a November 9, 2007 letter he authored as Principal Deputy AAG for Legislative Affairs to the House Judiciary Committee, arguing that “the Department is not aware of any reasons why state and local authorities are not currently able to pursue prostitution-related crimes such that Federal jurisdiction is necessary.” Kirkland & Ellis's formal submission to the Deputy AG defending Epstein [EFTA00013811] cited this letter to argue that Epstein's conduct should not be federally prosecuted under 18 USC 1591, 2422(b), or 2423(b). K&E used Benczkowski's own words — written in his official DOJ capacity — to support its argument against federal prosecution of their client.

The second documented link came in 2008, when Benczkowski served as Chief of Staff to Deputy AG Mark Filip. During this period, K&E partner Ken Starr wrote directly to Filip, accusing prosecutors of misconduct and urging DOJ Main Justice intervention against the Epstein federal case. Benczkowski held the chief of staff role in Filip's office while this lobbying campaign was underway.

The third and broadest link is temporal. Benczkowski headed the DOJ Criminal Division from July 2018 to July 2020, a period encompassing the entire SDNY Epstein prosecution — from indictment (July 6, 2019) through death (August 10, 2019) and the continuing investigation. The Criminal Division's Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section (CEOS) is the federal unit responsible for sex trafficking cases under 18 USC 1591. Yet a search of the entire 331,000+ DOJ document corpus returns zero results for “Benczkowski.” The AAG overseeing the division with institutional responsibility for this case does not appear in any recovered case files. Whether this reflects formal recusal, deliberate distance, or archival gaps remains an open question.

sections.title: Alfa Bank, Confirmation, and Undisclosed Conflicts
sections.content:
In March 2017, K&E partner Viet Dinh brought Benczkowski into the representation of Alfa Bank, Russia’s largest private bank, controlled by oligarchs Mikhail Fridman, Petr Aven, and German Khan. Benczkowski oversaw the hiring of Stroz Friedberg to conduct a computer forensics investigation of Alfa Bank servers, examining whether hackers had fabricated a cyber trail suggesting communications between Alfa Bank and the Trump Organization. He also advised on a potential defamation case against BuzzFeed over publication of the Steele dossier. The work ran from March to early June 2017; his nomination for AAG Criminal Division came almost immediately after.

The confirmation process exposed disclosure failures. Benczkowski omitted the Alfa Bank representation from his Senate questionnaire; it was discovered only in his FBI background file. He claimed K&E’s confidentiality agreement prevented disclosure. His recusal was narrowly drawn to Alfa Bank matters specifically, excluding the broader Alfa Group Consortium, and he refused to commit to recusal from the Mueller investigation or other Russia-related matters. Two confidential clients appeared on his financial disclosure — one involved in a non-public investigation. He was confirmed 51–48 on July 11, 2018, with all Democrats opposed and Senators Whitehouse, Warner, Coons, and Durbin leading the opposition.

A previously unconnected dimension of the Alfa Bank conflict emerged from the DOJ document corpus: Alfa Bank was an actual financial intermediary used by the Epstein operation for international wire transfers. At least ten documents in the LMSBAND corpus contain wire instructions to Alfa Bank Moscow (SWIFT: ALFARUMM) via Bank of New York Mellon and Wells Fargo as US correspondents. EFTA02629196 documents a January/February 2019 wire to Alfa Bank handled by Richard Kahn, with Bella Klein noting that “wire was held up as intermediary US bank is required for USD wires to Alfa Bank.” The dual function of Alfa Bank — as both Benczkowski’s K&E client and as an Epstein financial conduit — was never publicly connected during the confirmation process. Alfa Bank had zero FARA registrations despite its owners’ status as known political actors.

sections.title: Ethics Waivers and the 1MDB Prosecution
sections.content:
Benczkowski's Criminal Division tenure involved a series of ethics waivers that allowed him to participate in prosecutions of K&E clients. He received at least three waivers: one in November 2018 for the Goldman Sachs 1MDB case, a second in April 2019 for the same matter, and a third in December 2019 for an unspecified “confidential criminal matter.” AG Barr received a parallel 1MDB waiver.

The Goldman Sachs case illustrates the revolving door in practice. Goldman's lead K&E defense counsel was Mark Filip — Benczkowski's former boss at DOJ and longtime K&E co-counsel. Filip argued that Goldman should not be prosecuted. Goldman ultimately paid $2.9 billion but avoided a guilty plea. Critics, including CREW (Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington), argued the waivers enabled lenient treatment of the firm. In this arrangement, the government official deciding whether to prosecute the firm had received $847,500 from the same law firm defending the target, and his longtime mentor was lead defense counsel.

Benczkowski's spouse's lobbying firm, West Front Strategies LLC, generated additional conflicts during this period. With 20+ lobbying filings, the firm represented Comcast, Microsoft, Expedia, Prudential Financial, T-Mobile, Walgreens, Best Buy, and Republic Services on issues including financial regulation, taxation, and telecommunications. Per ProPublica financial disclosures, the firm generated $500K–$1M annually while Benczkowski headed the Criminal Division, which has jurisdiction over corporate fraud and financial crimes affecting his spouse's clients' industries.

sections.title: Boeing and the Post-Government Capstone
sections.content:
In September 2025, Benczkowski joined Boeing as Vice President and Assistant General Counsel for Government Operations, managing the company's relationships with the same government agencies he had led or staffed at DOJ. The appointment came four months after Boeing's 737 MAX criminal case was resolved via a non-prosecution agreement in May 2025.

Boeing's criminal case connects to the Epstein investigation through Mark Filip. Filip, Benczkowski's former boss and K&E co-counsel, served as Boeing's lead defense attorney. Filip negotiated the original January 2021 deferred prosecution agreement (a $2.5 billion penalty with no guilty plea and no monitor, despite 346 deaths in two crashes). Legal scholar Paul Cassell argued that Boeing's DPA Statement of Facts was “ghostwritten by Boeing attorneys, in the same clubby fashion” as the Epstein NPA. Filip authored the “Filip Memorandum” governing DPA procedures while serving as Deputy AG, then used those same procedures to defend Boeing as K&E counsel, securing terms that critics compared to the Epstein deal his office had approved a decade earlier.

When Boeing breached the DPA in 2024, the case was resolved with a new NPA rather than the prosecution that typically follows a breach. Benczkowski was hired to manage the post-resolution relationship. FEC records confirm the transition: his biweekly donations shifted from K&E to Boeing PAC in late 2025. His Republican donor network includes contributions to Tom Cotton ($5K), Adam Laxalt ($2.9K), James Comer ($5K), and Ron DeSantis via Restore Our Nation PAC ($2.9K).

open_questions: What was Benczkowski's specific role, if any, in the Criminal Division's handling of the Epstein prosecution from July 2019 onward? His absence from 331,000+ documents could indicate formal recusal, SDNY bypassing Main Justice, or archival gaps. DOJ institutional protocols governing AAG involvement in CEOS cases would clarify which explanation applies.

What were the two confidential clients listed on Benczkowski's financial disclosure, one of whom was involved in a non-public investigation? K&E's confidentiality agreement blocked disclosure during the confirmation process, and these remain unidentified.
What was the scope of the December 2019 ethics waiver for an unspecified "confidential criminal matter"? This third waiver, beyond the two Goldman Sachs 1MDB waivers, has not been publicly explained.

Did Benczkowski have awareness of or involvement in the Starr-to-Filip lobbying campaign on the Epstein case while serving as Filip's Chief of Staff in 2008? The DAG chief of staff typically manages the office's incoming correspondence and briefing materials.

What is the full scope of Alfa Bank's role as a financial intermediary for Epstein wire transfers, and was any connection drawn between this role and Benczkowski's prior K&E representation of Alfa Bank during his ethics review?
